stories.title: Parambak ditoy MMSU 2025 Showcases Extension Technologies for Farmers

images.caption: 7th Parambak ditoy MMSU, in front of CAFSD, 14 February 2025. (Photo: MMSU STRATCOM)

paras: On February 14, 2025, to close its 47th Foundation Anniversary, MMSU held the 7th Parambak ditoy MMSU in front of the College of Agriculture, Food and Sustainable Development, highlighting the impact of its extension and research programmes on community development and agricultural innovation. Thirty-seven exhibitors took part, including learning sites of the Agricultural Training Institute–Ilocos Region, Magsasaka Siyentista (farmer scientists), Balik-Probinsya beneficiaries and local government units, and the Research Directorate gave a speed talk on MMSU technologies such as off-season tomato and shallot production, Bolinao chicken, indigenous vegetables and black garlic.

Participants harvested fresh vegetables at the President’s Farm, 17 new partners of the Extension Directorate received certificates of appreciation, and beneficiaries shared how MMSU’s technologies had supported sustainable agriculture. Attendees included the Provincial Government of Ilocos Norte, LGUs, non-government organisations, farmer leaders, entrepreneurs and MMSU-assisted beneficiaries. Incoming President Virgilio Julius P. Manzano Jr. urged the units concerned to sustain sustainable farming practices.
sources: MMSU Extension Directorate, “‘Parambak’ caps MMSU@47 celebration,” February 2025  https://extension.mmsu.edu.ph/news/show/368/parambak-caps-mmsu-at-47-celebration

stories.title: CAFSD Graduands Plant Native Trees and Bamboo in the University Forest Reserves

images.caption: CAFSD Graduating Class 2025 “Bamboo and Tree Planting Activity,” University Forest Reserves, City of Batac, 2 July 2025. (Photo: MMSU STRATCOM)
Bamboo planting site in the University Forest Reserve, Brgy. Mabaleng, 2 July 2025. (Photo: MMSU STRATCOM)

paras: Some 230 graduating students of the College of Agriculture, Food and Sustainable Development (CAFSD) of Mariano Marcos State University (MMSU) planted trees and bamboo in the University Forest Reserves in Barangays Payao and Mabaleng, City of Batac, on July 2, 2025. The activity was led by CAFSD OIC-Dean Charlie Batin and the 2025 CAFSD Graduating Class Student Council, with Dr. Joselito Rosario, Director for Agribusiness, and Mr. Bonne Jovie Orteza of the MMSU Bamboo Research and Development Center. MMSU President Virgilio Julius P. Manzano Jr. commended the class for leaving a lasting green footprint that will further preserve the forest areas managed by the university, and Mr. Hashler Garalde, a CAFSD alumnus representing the Provincial Government of Ilocos Norte, supported the college’s sustainability efforts.

The graduands planted 120 seedlings of guijo and yakal, native dipterocarp timber species raised at the MMSU Central Nursery, in the Payao Forest Reserve, and 130 propagules of kawayan tinik, machiku and giant bamboo from the MMSU Bamboo Nursery in Mabaleng.

stories.title: MMSU Plants 250 Mangrove Propagules in Currimao on World Environment Day

images.caption: Mangrove planting for World Environment Day, Brgy. Maglaoi, Currimao, June 2025. (Photo: MMSU STRATCOM)
MMSU, LGU Currimao, DENR and fisherfolk volunteers at the planting site, June 2025. (Photo: MMSU STRATCOM)

paras: In June 2025, in celebration of World Environment Day, Mariano Marcos State University planted 250 mangrove propagules along the coastal area of Barangay Maglaoi, Currimao, Ilocos Norte, to restore degraded shorelines, enhance climate resilience and promote sustainable coastal resource management. The activity was spearheaded by the MMSU Sustainability and Futures Thinking (SFT) Office with the Local Government Unit of Currimao and led by Dr. Mee Jay Domingo, Vice President for Planning and Strategic Foresight.

MMSU faculty, education support personnel and students joined representatives of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources, barangay officials, members of local fisherfolk organizations and community members. SFT Director Dr. Arlene Gonzales explained that mangroves were chosen because they act as natural filters that intercept plastic waste from land before it reaches the sea, while absorbing carbon, protecting shorelines from erosion and providing habitat for marine life.
sources: MMSU News, “MMSU plants 250 mangrove propagules in Currimao,” 11 June 2025  https://www.mmsu.edu.ph/news/mmsu-plants-250-mangrove-propagules-in-currimao

stories.title: Green Wall Program: Coconut Seedlings for the Currimao Coastline

images.caption: Forum series of the 2025 National Science and Technology Week, Northwestern University, Laoag City, 19 November 2025. (Photo: MMSU)

stories.title: President’s Farm Field Day Showcases Climate-Resilient Rice Varieties

images.caption: President’s Farm technology demonstration of inbred and hybrid rice varieties, 28 October 2025. (Photo: MMSU)
Farmers, LGU technicians and students at the President’s Farm Field Day, in front of CAFSD. (Photo: MMSU)

paras: On October 28, 2025, the MMSU Extension Directorate, with the Philippine Rice Research Institute (PhilRice) Batac Branch, held the President’s Farm Field Day: A Technology Showcase in front of the College of Agriculture, Food and Sustainable Development. Farmers and farmer-leaders, agricultural technicians from Ilocos Norte local government units, BS Agriculture students, and MMSU and PhilRice rice specialists viewed eight rice varieties grown under wet-season conditions.

The varieties included four newly released by PhilRice, two public hybrids, and two suited to saline and rainfed conditions, among them NSIC Rc 686 (Salinas 39) and NSIC Rc 650 (Sahod Ulan 36), giving farmers options for saline-affected and rainfed fields. Speakers included MMSU President Dr. Virgilio Julius P. Manzano Jr., Extension Director Dr. Marlowe Aquino, and former MMSU President and PhilRice Executive Director Dr. Santiago R. Obien.
sources: MMSU News, “MMSU President’s Farm showcases 8 rice varieties,” 4 November 2025  https://www.mmsu.edu.ph/article/news/2665/mmsu-presidents-farm-showcases-8-rice-varieties

stories.title: 2025 International Day for Biological Diversity Wildlife Photo Contest

images.caption: Contest poster with the animal-photography ethical guidelines (deadline 30 May 2025).
Winner Chris Jeremiah C. Antonio receives his certificate from Dr. Arlene L. Gonzales, Chief of Sustainability and Futures Thinking.

paras: MMSU, through its Office of Sustainability and Futures Thinking, marked the 2025 International Day for Biological Diversity with a Wildlife Photo Contest that invited the university community to document local wildlife and promote awareness of biodiversity conservation. Entrants followed animal-photography ethical guidelines: avoiding flash and loud noises, never using bait or food lures, following local laws and warning signs, keeping clear of nesting sites and sensitive habitats, and captioning photographs honestly. Entries were received until May 30, 2025.

Chris Jeremiah C. Antonio, a third-year BA Communication student, was named winner and received a ₱1,000 gift voucher and a certificate from Dr. Arlene L. Gonzales, Chief of Sustainability and Futures Thinking.
sources: MMSU SDG 15 Life on Land report (2025), Office of Sustainability and Futures Thinking

stories.title: Graduation Tree Planting Is a Standing MMSU Programme, 2024 to 2026

images.caption: CAFSD Graduating Class 2026 enrichment planting at the MMSU Forest Reserve, Payao, 1 June 2026. (Photo: MMSU STRATCOM)

paras: Graduating classes of the College of Agriculture, Food and Sustainable Development (CAFSD) of Mariano Marcos State University (MMSU) plant trees before they graduate, and the planting has been repeated every year. On July 9, 2024, the BS Forestry graduating class, led by CAFSD OIC-Dean Charlie Batin, enriched the Salinged Park, the university’s ecological park, with igem-dagat, balitbitan, bitaog, Cassia javanica and banaba. On July 2, 2025, 230 CAFSD graduands planted guijo, yakal and bamboo in the University Forest Reserves in Payao and Mabaleng, City of Batac.

On June 1, 2026, the CAFSD Graduating Class of 2026, led by its Student Council with the chairs and faculty of the Departments of Environmental Science and Forestry, carried out an enrichment planting at the MMSU Forest Reserve in Payao, which the CAFSD Batch 2025 had previously planted with native seedlings. They planted 50 banaba, 30 yakal saplungan and 20 guijo seedlings at the onset of the rainy season, hardened in the MMSU Forest Tree Nursery, species chosen because they improve soil quality, conserve biodiversity and absorb and store carbon dioxide. Dr. Arlene Gonzales, Director of the Sustainability and Futures Thinking Office, represented the University President and commended the college for sustaining the initiative. The activity follows Republic Act 10800, the Graduation Legacy for the Environment Act, which requires students to plant trees before graduation.

stories.title: New Research Greenhouse and Staff Training Support Controlled-Environment Crop Production on Campus

images.caption: MMSU researchers and farm workers train on the new greenhouse at the RDE complex, 13 May 2025. (Photo: MMSU Research Directorate)

paras: On May 13, 2025, eighteen researchers and farm workers of Mariano Marcos State University took part in hands-on training on the operation and management of the newly constructed greenhouse in the university’s research, development and extension (RDE) complex. The training, facilitated by the project contractor as part of the turnover, covered the basic functions and systems of the greenhouse and crop-specific management strategies; a follow-up session on May 20, 2025 covered the preparation of planting solutions for soilless and hydroponic systems.

The Php 2.2-million facility measures 10 by 6 metres and 6.1 metres high, uses combined mechanical and natural ventilation, and has an integrated planting system in three bays for soilless cultivation, hydroponics and soil-based planting. It was built under the Higher Education Reform and Innovation Program (HERIP) to strengthen research in controlled-environment agriculture and to give students immersive learning.

stories.title: Conserving Ilocos Indigenous Food Plants In Situ, Ex Situ and Circa Situ

images.caption: Partners receive indigenous food plant planting materials for the Community Foodscapes and Seedbanks, World Food Day 2025.

paras: Through its Indigenous Food Plants (IFP) Program, MMSU conserves the wild and neglected food plants of Ilocos Norte, 46 of which were documented by the program in seven towns of the province. The program follows a triad of conservation approaches: an IFP Botanical Garden for ex situ conservation, a himbabao (alukon) genebank at the MMSU Forest Reserve, circa situ cultivation of the wild yams kamangeg and dolian, and the integration of IFPs into community foodscapes.

In October 2025, in celebration of World Food Day, the MMSU Extension and Research Directorates established the second batch of Community Foodscapes and Seedbanks for Indigenous Food Plants with local government units and schools, at Eladio V. Barangan Memorial Elementary School in San Nicolas, Ilocos Norte. The foodscape sites serve as seedbanks and learning gardens, and partner communities receive planting materials and technical assistance to cultivate kapaskapas, alokon, pako, dalayap, wild singkamas and roselle. The new partners join existing foodscape sites in Sarrat and Batac.

The IFP Program was adopted by the Regional Development Council of Region 1 as its first research and development initiative, and a study on the program by Dr. Menisa A. Antonio and co-authors won Best Paper in the Sustainable and Smart Agri-Aquaculture and Climate Resilience category of the SUC-ACAP 2025 Biennial Conference, held August 27–29, 2025, in Tagbilaran City, Bohol.
sources: MMSU Research Directorate, “MMSU research on indigenous food plants wins best paper at SUC-ACAP 2025 Conference,” 29 August 2025  https://research.mmsu.edu.ph/news/details/mmsu-research-on-indigenous-food-plants-wins-best-paper-at-suc-acap-2025-conference

stories.title: Nature-based Solutions for Mangrove Ecosystems in Badoc and Currimao

images.caption: Mangrove site, from the gallery of the October 2025 seminar-workshop of the NbS mangrove project. (Photo: MMSU)
Dr. Arlene L. Gonzales at the MMSU–DENR Region 1 dialogue on mangrove conservation, ILAARRDEC.

paras: Throughout 2025, MMSU implemented the DOST-PCAARRD-funded project “Nature-based Solutions (NbS) for Sustainable Mangrove Management and Resilient Coastal Communities Through Innovative Green Engineering Approach,” led by Dr. Arlene L. Gonzales, in Badoc and Currimao, Ilocos Norte, with DENR-PENRO Ilocos Norte, the Provincial Government of Ilocos Norte and the LGUs of Badoc and Currimao. The project uses green engineering and locally available, ecologically friendly materials, including bamboo-engineered structures that protect young mangroves and improve their survival.

In 2025, MMSU and DENR Region 1 met at ILAARRDEC to advance the work, with DENR pledging technical support and active participation in restoration, monitoring and evaluation, and the project trained representatives of Currimao, Pasuquin, Badoc and Burgos in mangrove propagation, management and conservation on October 27–28, 2025.

The MMSU project team with DOST-PCAARRD, DENR-PENRO Ilocos Norte, the Provincial Government of Ilocos Norte and the LGUs of Badoc and Currimao at the launch. (Image credit: TTPD, DOST-PCAARRD)

Gonzales of MMSU, was launched at the MMSU Review Center on June 27, 2024, and runs from May 1, 2024 to April 30, 2026 in Badoc and Currimao, Ilocos Norte. DENR-PENRO Ilocos Norte, the Provincial Government of Ilocos Norte and the local government units of Badoc and Currimao support the project.

stories.title: Bambusetums Create Living Collections for Bamboo Conservation and Learning

images.caption: Launch of the bambusetum at the MMSU Dingras Campus, 30 September 2026. (Photo: MMSU STRATCOM)

paras: In celebration of Bamboo Month, the MMSU Dingras Campus, through CAFSD, launched its bambusetum on September 30, 2026, to advance bamboo research, education and sustainable use. Students, faculty, field workers and stakeholders joined the planting, where For. Charlie Maine Cacactin demonstrated the proper planting of various bamboo species, and members of the Association of Young Agriculturists, Green Triangle Organization, Health and Wellness Club and Junior Foresters’ Association supported the activity. The bambusetum is the second in the university, after the one at the Main Campus.

The bambusetum will serve as a living collection of bamboo species and a learning site for teaching, research, technology development and community extension, showcasing bamboo’s ecological and socioeconomic benefits for food security, livelihood, environmental conservation and climate resilience. It follows the bambusetum that training participants established in Barangay Aglipay, Pinili, in 2025. CAFSD Dean Charlie Batin said the work responds to environmental problems such as climate change.

paras: On May 2, 2025, the MMSU Research and Extension Directorates trained 64 farmers in Barangay 11 Sta. Rosa, Sarrat, Ilocos Norte, on the propagation of alukon (himbabao), a Philippine indigenous vegetable tree. Barangay officials, members of the Task Force Dagger Special Operations Foundation and representatives of the local government unit also attended. The training was held in response to requests from the community.

Resource speakers Dr. Menisa Antonio, Engr. Josefa Pugat and Mr. Jayson Rasay of the Research Directorate presented recommended propagation strategies to establish sustained alukon production in the community and broaden the use of the crop for food and other applications.

paras: Through its Information and Technology Caravan, MMSU’s Research and Extension Directorates joined the 2025 Siwawer Farmers’ Festival and Agro-Trade Fair at the Vintar Public Auditorium on December 3–4, 2025, with an exhibit of university technologies and a series of expert lectures for farmers.

Forester Shena Rose Garcia introduced sustainable bamboo production using MMSU’s one-node cutting technology, and the second day featured a demonstration on the propagation of alukon, an indigenous vegetable tree, facilitated by Ms. Josefa Pugat. paras: A new season of the MMSU School-on-the-Air (SOA), the university’s radio-based educational program, opened on June 24 and 25, 2025 with 1,000 enrollees from the 22 municipalities and cities of Ilocos Norte. The season focused on regenerative vegetable farming for enhanced and sustainable production, with lessons on climate-smart practices and off-season vegetable seeding.

MMSU ran the program with the Provincial Government of Ilocos Norte, the Office of the Provincial Agriculturist, local government units, the Ilocos Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development Consortium, and the High-Value Crops Division of Ilocos Norte.

Attendees included the Provincial Government of Ilocos Norte, LGUs, non-government organisations, farmer leaders, entrepreneurs and MMSU-assisted beneficiaries. Incoming President Virgilio Julius P. stories.title: Bamboo Propagation and Plantation Management Training in Pinili

images.caption: Participants of the bamboo propagation, nursery and plantation management training, Brgy. Aglipay, Pinili, 2025. (Photo: MMSU)

stories.title: Vermicast Facility Helps Pasuquin Onion Farmers Restore Degraded Soils

images.caption: Pilot vermicomposting facility of Pasuquin white onion farmers, 2025. (Photo: MMSU STRATCOM)

paras: In 2025, white onion farmer-leaders Mr. Marcos Palacay and Mr. Markflor Valdez of the Ayat ti Pasuquin Farmer and Irrigators Association established a pilot vermicomposting facility in Pasuquin, Ilocos Norte, under the Agri-Tech Facilitator Program of the Farmers Entrepreneurship Program of MMSU and the Jollibee Group Foundation. The facility uses African night crawlers (Eudrilus eugeniae) to convert biodegradable farm waste into vermicast, an organic fertilizer that improves soil structure, stimulates microbial activity and reduces the need for chemical inputs.

The project responds to soil degradation from prolonged reliance on chemical fertilizers, which the farmers linked to poor soil conditions and low seedling survival, and promotes sustainable solutions for white onion farming in the area.

paras: On October 28, 2025, the MMSU Extension Directorate, with the Philippine Rice Research Institute (PhilRice) Batac Branch, held the President’s Farm Field Day: A Technology Showcase in front of the College of Agriculture, Food and Sustainable Development. Farmers and farmer-leaders, agricultural technicians from Ilocos Norte local government units, BS Agriculture students, and MMSU and PhilRice rice specialists viewed eight rice varieties grown under wet-season conditions.

The varieties included four newly released by PhilRice, two public hybrids, and two suited to saline and rainfed conditions, among them NSIC Rc 686 (Salinas 39) and NSIC Rc 650 (Sahod Ulan 36), giving farmers options for saline-affected and rainfed fields. stories.title: MMSU Leads Soil Health Research for Rice-Based Cropping Systems

images.caption: Kick-off meeting of the soil health management project with Griffith University and provincial agriculturists, 16 June 2025. (Photo: MMSU STRATCOM)

paras: In 2025, MMSU became a key partner in a five-year research program led by Griffith University in Australia and funded by the Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research (ACIAR) and DOST-PCAARRD to develop soil knowledge, information and capacity for more productive and sustainable cropping systems in the Philippines (Project SLaM 2023/146). MMSU President Virgilio Julius P. Manzano Jr. pledged the university’s commitment at the inception meeting held March 24–26, 2025 in Balanga City, Bataan.

MMSU leads the project on enhancing the productivity of rice-based cropping systems in Ilocos Norte, Tarlac and Bataan through soil health management. Led by Dr. Janet Villamor, it evaluates nutrient management practices and develops yield-calibrated soil health indices for rice-garlic, rice-rice and rice-onion systems. The kick-off meeting on June 16, 2025 at the MMSU Center for Flexible Learning brought together Griffith University, the country project manager and the provincial agriculturists of Ilocos Norte, Bataan and Tarlac, with visits to project sites in Batac, Vintar and Pasuquin.

stories.title: MMSU Land Use Policy Commits the University to Conserve and Restore Its Lands

images.caption: Document: MMSU Land Use, Zoning, Water and Energy Policies (Sirmata 2040 LUDIP, 2021), Land Use Policy, page 1.

paras: MMSU’s Land Use, Zoning, Water and Energy Policies, adopted as part of Sirmata 2040, the university’s Land Use Development and Infrastructure Plan prepared in 2021 under Republic Act 11396, govern the conservation, restoration and sustainable use of all university lands across its campuses.

Under Policy 1.3, the allocation and use of university lands “shall aim to maintain, protect, conserve, restore, and enhance the integrity of the land itself, the environment and ecological balance in all its campuses.” Policy 7.1 requires decisions to be based on valid and reliable science, especially for any intent to alter or convert the natural state of any piece of university land, and Policy 10.2 gives fragile lands and protected areas special management “to protect, conserve, enrich, rehabilitate, and or sustain them.”

The zoning policy sets aside Protected Land as a distinct zone; under Policy 9.1, “protected landholdings of the university shall be conserved, preserved and to be excluded from any form of alteration except as may be permitted by operation of law.” The MMSU Forest Reserve is maintained as a no-build zone, and Policy 4.3 requires the university to regularly review, update and promptly communicate its land-use policies.

stories.title: From Vanishing Plants to Regional Policy: MMSU Identifies, Conserves and Monitors Threatened Indigenous Food Plants

images.caption: Farmers and local officials trained on alukon (himbabao) propagation, Brgy. 11 Sta. Rosa, Sarrat, 2 May 2025. (Photo: MMSU)
Partners receive indigenous food plant planting materials for the Community Foodscapes and Seedbanks, World Food Day 2025.

paras: Mariano Marcos State University has long identified the plants of Ilocos Norte that are at risk of disappearing. In 2003, MMSU researchers, among them Dr. Miriam Pascua, Ms. Menisa Antonio and Dr. Dionisio Bucao, surveyed Laoag City, Batac, Pasuquin, San Nicolas and Dingras to document plants that elders perceived to be vanishing. Of the 124 plants named, 77 were validated as vanishing by the university’s agronomists and horticulturists using criteria of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN): 45 were classified as endangered and 32 as vulnerable, among them sugod-sugod (Momordica cochinchinensis), kapas-kapas and bignay (Antidesma bunius).

In 2011, the Southeast Asian Regional Center for Graduate Study and Research in Agriculture (SEARCA) published a study by MMSU researchers, “Survey and Characterization of Indigenous Food Plants in Ilocos Norte, Philippines” by Menisa A. Antonio, Rodel T. Utrera, Epifania O. Agustin, Dionisio L. Jamias, Araceli J. Badar and Miriam E. Pascua. Warning that indigenous food plants are disappearing at an alarming rate, the study documented 46 indigenous food plants from 27 plant families in seven upland and remote municipalities of Ilocos Norte, most of them wild species, recorded their identity, uses and locations, and reported that MMSU collects their germplasm and maintains it as living plants and seeds.

This work grew into MMSU’s Indigenous Food Plants (IFP) Program, led by Dr. Menisa A. Antonio of the Research Directorate, which documents IFP species in Ilocos Norte and protects them through a triad of conservation approaches: the IFP Botanical Garden (ex situ), a himbabao (alukon) genebank at the MMSU Forest Reserve, circa situ cultivation of the wild yams kamangeg and dolian, and the integration of indigenous food plants into community foodscapes. The program is also advancing omics-based molecular characterization to support their conservation and use. In 2025 it trained 64 farmers and local officials in Sarrat on the propagation of alukon (May 2, 2025) and extended its community seedbanks and foodscapes to new partner barangays in Vintar (October 2025), and its paper “From wild foods to policy innovation: MMSU’s indigenous food plants program as a model for sustainable and inclusive agriculture” won Best Paper at the 2025 SUC-ACAP Biennial Conference (August 27–29, 2025).

The IFP Program is the first research and development initiative adopted by the Regional Development Council (RDC) of Region 1, providing input for policy advocacy on the conservation and use of these species. Implementation continues: on June 6, 2026, the Philippine News Agency reported that indigenous food plants such as sugod-sugod, alokon, buga and karot are propagated at the botanical garden of the MMSU Natural Resources Conservation and Management Center and shared with schools and communities for food gardens.

stories.title: Sirmata 2040: Planning MMSU’s Campuses and Reserve Lands for Two Decades

images.caption: Document: MMSU Zoning Policy, Protected Land (Principle 9, Policy 9.1), Sirmata 2040 LUDIP.

paras: Sirmata 2040, MMSU’s Land Use Development and Infrastructure Plan (LUDIP), is the university’s 20-year guide for managing its land resources and infrastructure. Prepared under Republic Act 11396, which requires state universities and colleges to have a LUDIP, and supported by a Php 2 million grant from the Commission on Higher Education (CHED), the plan covers the future land use of the MMSU campuses and the university’s reserve areas in Nagbacsan, Payao, Lubbot and Sarnap, City of Batac, including the forest reserves where MMSU’s forestry and agroforestry research is set up.

Local biodiversity is built into the plan’s development rules. The zoning plan sets aside Protected Land, which “shall be conserved, preserved and to be excluded from any form of alteration except as may be permitted by operation of law” (Policy 9.1), and the MMSU Forest Reserve is kept as a no-build zone. Before any land is altered or converted, the plan requires a science-based assessment of its natural suitability and carrying capacity (Policies 7.1, 10.1 and 11.1).
The plan was developed through stakeholder consultations, sectoral studies and campus planning workshops, and was endorsed by the CHED Technical Working Group after validation visits to the campuses.

stories.title: Groundwater Quality Monitoring at the MMSU Farm

images.caption: Document: Groundwater Quality Assessment of the MMSU Farm, spatial variation of pH (monitoring through June 2025).

paras: Through June 2025, MMSU continued monthly monitoring of 17 groundwater wells on the MMSU Farm, measuring pH, total dissolved solids, electrical conductivity, chloride and nitrate-nitrogen and comparing the results with the Philippine National Standards for Drinking Water (2017). The assessment, covering February 2024 to June 2025, flags wells with persistently high dissolved solids, which rose again from January to May 2025, for continued monitoring to guide water resource management and prevent further degradation of groundwater quality.

Mean pH from February to December 2024 ranged from 6.75 to 7.69, within the 6.5–8.5 guideline of the national drinking water standards. Small campus reservoirs also collect rainwater, reduce flooding and recharge groundwater.

paras: On September 30, 2026, University President Virgilio Julius P. Manzano Jr. issued Memorandum No. 26-370 to all employees, adopting the University Environmental Compliance and Pollution Prevention Program under Republic Act 6969 (Toxic Substances and Hazardous and Nuclear Wastes Control Act), Republic Act 8749 (Clean Air Act), Republic Act 9275 (Clean Water Act), Republic Act 9003 (Ecological Solid Waste Management Act) and Presidential Decree 1586 (Environmental Impact Statement System). The memorandum covers the management of hazardous wastes, wastewater, air emissions, solid wastes and chemicals, together with permits, monitoring, reporting and inspections required by the Department of Environment and Natural Resources – Environmental Management Bureau (DENR-EMB), and directs all offices, colleges, laboratories, research units and auxiliary enterprises to comply with the attached Environmental Compliance Procedures.

The attached procedure for PCB-containing and potentially PCB-containing electrical equipment, such as transformers, capacitors, voltage regulators, circuit breakers, reclosers and oil-filled switches, requires every unit to inventory its equipment and submit the inventory to the Sustainability and Futures Thinking (SFT) Office. The SFT Office validates the inventory, keeps the university’s central PCB inventory and the DENR-EMB online PCB inventory, ensures labelling, conducts inspections and annual inventory validation, and prepares the reports required by DENR-EMB. No covered equipment may be relocated, transferred, repaired through oil handling, decommissioned, condemned or disposed of without the SFT Office’s written clearance, and PCB wastes and equipment may be disposed of only through DENR-accredited transporters, treaters and disposal facilities. The SFT Office keeps hazardous waste manifests and certificates of treatment or disposal among its records.

paras: MMSU’s Integrated Waste Management Program was revised in 2020 into the Integrated Pollution and Waste Management Program (IPWMP), implemented by the Pollution Control Unit and the General Services directorate, to cover hazardous materials. The IPWMP assigns focal persons for hazardous wastes (chemical and related wastes), air and water pollution, solid wastes, and PCBs and related industrial wastes, and requires the waste coordinators of every unit to store and label generated hazardous wastes properly before collection.

The program establishes centralized, separate storage facilities for polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) and other hazardous or toxic wastes collected from the campuses, where the wastes are kept for up to one year before disposal through a DENR-accredited transport, storage and disposal facility, in compliance with Republic Act 6969 and its storage guidelines. Units that generate hazardous waste are registered as hazardous waste generators, and the university coordinates with the Environmental Management Bureau of DENR for final collection and disposal.
